adversarial_test_results.prompt: The museum's shell collection had sat in storage since the flood of 1953, when the basement of the old customs house took on nearly two metres of river water. Volunteers spent four winters lifting drawers of shells, drying labels, and copying accession numbers into a database that had been written for coins. Most of the material proved ordinary: mussels from the estuary, cockles from the sandbanks, and a long series of winkles that a Victorian curator had arranged by size rather than by species. The interesting boxes were at the back, wrapped in newspaper, and these had clearly belonged to a private collector whose name appeared nowhere in the catalogue. The labels were written in a small, cramped hand, sometimes in ink and sometimes in pencil, and they recorded places rather than dates: a bay in the Hebrides, a market in Naples, a river mouth in Mozambique. The paper had yellowed unevenly, so corners crumbled when touched, and the volunteers learned to photograph every label before lifting it. In the fifth winter a retired zoologist joined the team and began sorting the collection by locality. She noticed that shells from the tropics were wrapped in pages of a Portuguese newspaper, while the northern material came in pages of an Edinburgh daily. That suggested at least two journeys, and perhaps two collectors. The accession ledger, however, mentioned only one donation, received in 1903 from an unnamed donor. She traced the newspaper to a shipping company that had run a regular service between Lisbon and the Cape, and then, more slowly, to the family of the company's agent. The family had kept a trunk of correspondence, and in it were letters describing a young naturalist who had spent three years on the coast collecting shells and pressing plants. The letters gave no surname and signed only a first name, but they mentioned a cousin in the Cape Colony who had helped to pack the boxes and who had paid for the freight. One envelope held a photograph of a bare room with a table, a lamp, and rows of glass jars. Nothing in the ledger matched the dates in the letters, and the accession number on the largest box had been written twice, in two different inks. The volunteers began to suspect that the donation had been assembled from several smaller gifts and entered under a single date to satisfy the paperwork. A note in the margin, in a third hand, mentioned a shipment delayed by storms and a second shipment lost entirely. None of this explained the tropical shells, which were the finest in the collection and which had clearly been packed with great care. The zoologist drafted a short article for the local journal, describing the shells and asking whether any reader recognised the handwriting. She received two replies, both cautious. The first pointed to a family of merchants in Edinburgh; the second, from a retired archivist in Cape Town, was more specific. It said that the handwriting resembled that of a young man who had kept a shop near the harbour in the 1890s and who had corresponded with several collectors in Europe. The archivist offered to check a box of papers in the church archive. Three months later a photocopy arrived. It showed a single leaf torn from a ledger, with a column of figures and, at the foot of the page, a name. The name was Bwalya.
